In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
teachers’ attitudes toward AAE are not necessarily a product of individual beliefs or personal experiences, but are rather a product of the school environment and the school’s philosophy of language.

teachers who have had the benefit of training in African American English, and those who work in schools where there is a policy of respect and acceptance of the language, have a much more positive attitude towards African American English than those who have not had such training or who work in schools with little or no language policy.

teachers in schools with a policy that explicitly recognizes the legitimacy of African American English are more likely to have a positive attitude toward AAE than teachers in schools that have no policy on AAE or that have a negative policy.

school philosophy is an essential component for teachers to be sensitive to the needs of their students, and to be able to implement appropriate instructional strategies.
school policy and teachers’ attitudes toward AAE are inextricably linked.
school philosophy and school policy have a significant influence on teacher attitudes.

teachers’ attitudes toward AAE and their willingness to address the language needs of their AAE-speaking students vary according to the school’s philosophy of language.
teachers are more likely to be sensitized to the linguistic diversity in the classroom when the school is perceived to have a more open and inclusive philosophy.
